utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 16th of February, 2010. I would like to greet all the people present in this courtroom. I would like to greet Mr. Seselj, Mr. Marcussen, Mrs. Biersay, their associates, as well as all the people assisting us. I shall ask the Registrar to move into private session -- to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Chamber also decides to lift the confidential character of questions asked before except for a part whereby the witness could be identified. But the Chamber will look into that in detail and there shall be a decision very quickly about that. Let's proceed with the questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first we apologise about this interruption. Let's get back to this person from Novi Sad, if I understand you, who came to talk in Hrtkovci in a way which you said was peaceful. On whose behalf did he speak, on behalf of what political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what party that was. I can see the face of its leader, but I can't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's not present in the courtroom, is he, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In your statements you also mention another rally which allegedly took place in the spring of 1992 which you did not attend but which you talk as you heard about it and you heard about the significant parts of those -- of this rally. So I'd like you to tell us a little bit about this rally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you talk about it in your statements. This is not something which I'm suggesting out of the blue; this is something which arises from your statements. So can you please tell us about this rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that I did not attend the rally, but I know that of the major political figures in Serbia at the time, Ms. Pesic was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some other prominent figures, unfortunately I can't recall their names, were also there. As far as I know, one of the people there is a prominent member of a non-governmental organisation in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us which non-governmental organisation it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really tell you. I don't know the name of the institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know the name of the accused of this trial in which you're now giving your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he ever come to Hrtkovci in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did he ever come to Hrtkovci? Yes, in early May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At what exact date, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I stated the 6th of May, 1992, as the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. That is what is found in your statements. Now, Witness, you talked about this rally, of the speech allegedly made by Mr. Seselj there by hearsay because you did not attend it yourself. What I'm essentially interested in has to do with the question of the list. And essentially the fact that in the list, according to what you're saying, your name was also on this list. So can you confirm that you heard about a list of people who were supposed to go as quickly as possible, go away from Hrtkovci? I'm talking about Croats and Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can say again, as I stated before, I never laid eyes personally on that list and I had never read a name on that list of a Croat or a Croatian -- of a Croat or a Hungarian who was to leave Hrtkovci. I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a few people who attended the rally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Those were private conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you hear anybody say that someone had allegedly read out this list of names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I've heard, only a few names were read out. But I can only repeat again, I only heard about it because I did not attend the rally myself. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That we have understood, but I wanted to know something else. When you were told about this, namely that some names had been read out, names were on that list of people that needed to leave as quickly as possible and leave Hrtkovci, were you also told who read out this list at the rally? Or perhaps simply read out a few names on this list. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall that I was told who read out the names, but truth to tell, I did not consider that a very important piece of information. What I thought important was that such a list exists and that it contains names of people who were supposed to leave. Whether this or that person read out the list, I didn't think was important at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, yes, it is rather important in our eyes. Witness, I have another question for you. I'd like to know this. This is a sentence which purportedly had been mentioned during this rally. Can you remember this sentence and the author of this phrase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had rather you remember what you mentioned in your statements. I'm still talking about the fact that the people from different ethnic backgrounds, i.e., people who were not Serbs, needed to leave. Do you remember this, that they needed to leave Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was told that Mr. Seselj had said on that occasion that it would be better for Croats from Hrtkovci to leave the place while they still had the opportunity to leave under the circumstances that still prevailed, that means after having exchanged their properties with Serbs that were in a similar situation as we in Croatia or we would leave later with just the bare necessities in a small bag. I think that's what I said in my statement and it was from what I heard about the rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this sentence is fairly detailed, I'm asking you whether you remember who told you this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really can't tell you. It was a conversation among a number of people, people who had attended the rally where it was said. Now, who exactly quoted that sentence, I would be hard-put to remember now and I couldn't remember it even when I was giving the statement. One of these people but I didn't think it was important to try to remember who that was. What mattered to me was what was said, the substance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a few more minutes. I would like to address your personal situation now, with a degree of caution, of course, because we are now in open session. You left Hrtkovci, if I remember correctly, at the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You resigned from your job well before that, a month and a half or so before that, after this rally. I was wondering --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's leave the details aside because we wish to protect your identity. I was wondering why so much time elapsed between your resignation and your departure. Were you forced to resign from your job? Were you pressured in any way to resign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I said in my statement. There were no direct threats, no one person out of those who filed through Hrtkovci at the time and whom I considered to be Serb refugees or Serbs expelled from Croatia had ever threatened me in so many words or asked me to leave my job or the village of Hrtkovci. I believe that I said as much in my statement that I gave a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Hrtkovci, I and a lot of the people had a very good idea of what had happened in Vukovar and some Bosnian towns, that grave crimes had been committed including killing of non-Serbs. And the warnings that we were receiving and that were voiced aloud at the rally at Hrtkovci later and other rallies as well, including on the floor of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, I understood to be quite serious warnings in view of what had happened in Vukovar. And I thought that such warnings and those events could not be ignored. Therefore, I believed that in view of my ethnicity I could be a target and so could my family and that it was wise to take steps to remove that threat; and for me, that meant at the time moving to Croatia and swapping our property with some unfortunate person who at the time was a citizen of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, one last short question. Nonetheless, you said in your statements that your wife had received visits while you were not at home and that these visits indicated that you were being pressured to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can confirm only that my wife told me that. At that time, I was often away, travelling between Hrtkovci and some places in Croatia, mainly Zagreb and the environs of Zagreb. And she told me that there had been several visits by armed men who were threatening - would be the most precise word - in view of the guns they had and the things they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you. After that, I shall give the floor to Judge Harhoff. What I'm primarily interested in is this, this speech which purportedly was made and which people told you about, they told you about the content of this speech. What I want to know is: At the time when a rally of this nature was organised, did the local press mention it? Did the print press indicate that such a political meeting was going to be held, or on the 6th of May, 1992, was there not a single journalist present in this room? No one mentioned it, either on the radio or on television? What can you tell me about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the fact that the rally would be held, I really did not know, either from television or from newspapers, but rumours about this upcoming event had circulated around the village. I don't know who started these rumours, this talk, whether it was announced on television

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to redact what you have just said. So what did you learn in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that a rally would be held in Hrtkovci and that it would be attended by Mr. Seselj, who would also speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question: In your village at the time was there a local newspaper or was there no local newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no local newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no local newspaper. Did you yourself read --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I mean when you say local, I mean really local. That's how I understand it. I think I understood you correctly. No, we really did not have a local newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there articles in the national newspapers that talked about your village sometimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until that time, up until that date, I can't remember any except for one story in a Belgrade weekly called "Nin." And the story mentioned the Ustasha village of Hrtkovci, but that was a few years before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your 2006 statement you said that Mr. Seselj made speeches, political speeches, and that you had heard him. You said you also heard him on television, that it wasn't only him. You said there were other intellectuals also. This is my last question. Before the 6th of May, 1992, had you heard Mr. Seselj make political speeches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from what I remember, the Serbian television did not broadcast Seselj's speeches in their entirety. They broadcast only excerpts or short statements as part of a news item on the news bulletin. I really don't recall entire speeches by Mr. Seselj being broadcast on the television in Serbia. Some of the speeches were transmitted on local radio stations, but that again is something I heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall give the floor to my colleague who will put his questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Witness, I just have a few questions for you in extension of the thorough examination already conducted by my two colleagues. Could I begin by taking on where the Presiding Judge just left us, namely, in relation to the press coverage of the speeches made by Mr. Seselj. Because I would like to know if you are in a position to tell us whether the rally in Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, 1992, was covered by the press? Do you know if it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Newspapers wrote about it. I saw an article in the Belgrade daily "Borba."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear anything about the speech that Mr. Seselj held being broadcasted on either local or national radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Great. Now let me get back to the issue that was raised by Judge Lattanzi when she put questions to you about the list of names that were read out by someone during the rally. Because I think I remember from your statement that you said that you had heard that your name was also read out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said in my statement that my name was on that list, not that it was read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means somebody -- somebody who had a peep on that list told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. So your name was not read out, but you were told that your name did appear on the list. Now, how did that make you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To put it simply, it made me feel uncomfortable. The way I saw it, it was a threat and a sort of ultimatum that, quite simply, we must leave; in other words, if my name was on the list we should leave. And at that time I had no reason to believe that we were not on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. The reason I bring this up is that you also in your statement said that you did not receive any threats yourself. How are we to reconcile these two views? Did you mean to say that you never received any threats directly formulated directly towards you or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you please explain with a little more detail, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was giving that statement I meant to say that there was no direct threat, no demand in so many words by a person who would tell me so in my face that I had to go. And certainly it was not said in a threatening tone or intimidating language. Nobody told me in my face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. So your testimony is that you felt an indirect threat arriving out of the information that your name appeared on the list, but other than that, you did not encounter any direct threat. Is that the way we should understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could I then take you to another part in your statement, and indeed also bring you back to something that you have already explained to us in response to some questions put by Judge Lattanzi. It is the part where you said that you took the speech that was held by Mr. Seselj very seriously because you knew what had happened in Vukovar. And I'm referring to paragraph 17 of your statement from June 2004. And you go on to say that you "... heard very precisely what happened in Vukovar and there was no reasons for us not to believe Seselj's words." And I shall ask you to explain in a little more detail what exactly you meant by saying this. What did you -- what have you heard about the events that took place in Vukovar and how did this make you conclude that Mr. Seselj meant business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to say, first of all, a few words to the effect that we did hear about that and we had reliable information about what had happened in Vukovar. It's general knowledge that Vukovar was for the most part razed to the ground and many people were killed there, predominantly non-Serbs. Later I heard that quite a few Serbs also were killed there, but this is not the topic of our conversation here. We heard about the events at Ovcara, about the mass execution by firing squad of the captives there. This kind of information -- well, you could consider them to be rumours, but people from Hrtkovci had been conscripted into the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was still styled at the time, who claimed that having spent time in that area, they had heard or seen some things and that lots of people were killed there. On Sarajevo TV, this channel was called Yutel, we were able to see footage of Vukovar at the time and most of the footage showed piles of dead bodies. Now, the fact that some -- that numerous people were executed first in Vukovar and as I learned later on in some towns in Bosnia, I considered that to be a warning sign, something that one should not ignore, something that one should take into account very seriously. It was a serious warning that according to what Mr. Seselj had said at the rally in Hrtkovci, according to what I had been told about that, the warning and the instruction that we should leave Hrtkovci voluntarily while we could, I thought that all this should be taken very seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say "quite seriously." I don't mean to say that we were about to be executed in the same manner as it happened at those execution sites, but precisely what Mr. Seselj allegedly said, and that is that we would be forced to leave our homes with nothing but a small bag in our hands. At that time I considered that to be a serious threat, and I thought that my vital interests were threatened by statements such as that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if I really -- if I understood your question, that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You understood my question perfectly well and you also answered it very well. But, Mr. Witness, you may be aware that every hour and a half we have to take a short break because the tapes of the recordings from these proceedings need to be changed. So we will now take a break for 20 minutes, so we will resume ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now back in open session and Judge Harhoff will proceed with his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Before the break we were talking about the reasons why you wanted to take the message that you perceived coming out of Mr. Seselj's speech seriously because you had heard what happened in Vukovar. And you explained that very well. My next question to you would be just why you thought that what Mr. Seselj now said was to be given any weight. What made you think that exactly Mr. Seselj's speech was to be taken seriously? Did Mr. Seselj speak with any authority that demanded that his words were to be given particular importance? Why was it that of all the information that you may have heard at the time, Mr. Seselj's speech appeared to have a special impact on you? Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that at that time Mr. Seselj was or was considered to be a prominent political figure in Serbia. At the same time, the political party led by Mr. Seselj as far as I knew at the time had its armed wing, the paramilitary formations that took part in the fighting in Croatia and I assume also in Bosnia. If that information was correct, and indeed it proved to be correct later on, those paramilitary formations took part in the war events where things that could be or that I called executions happened. It is my opinion that those two facts contributed to Mr. Seselj's speech, the one that he held in Hrtkovci at the time, and some other speeches that I took note of either in the press or on TV. I considered that this speech, in light of those two facts, does have a considerable weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. You're being very clear. Can I just ask you to elaborate a little more on the first of these two elements that you have referred to. You said that the fact that Mr. Seselj was considered to be a prominent political figure in Serbia made you listen very attentively to what he said. In what sense was Mr. Seselj a prominent political figure in Serbia, and let me explain a little more what I'm trying to elicit from you. When Mr. Seselj spoke in public, did he express views that were consistent with what other prominent political figures in Serbia expressed at the time? Or was Mr. Seselj's views very much his own personal views that were individual to Mr. Seselj and were not necessarily shared by other persons in the political domain at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me first answer the part of the first question as to why I think that Mr. Seselj was a prominent figure on the political scene. At the time Mr. Seselj enjoyed a lot of media exposure for what he had to say, and he also had another platform to espouse his views in the Serbian Assembly. His party had a large following, and if I'm not mistaken, at that time it was between 10 and 15 per cent or maybe 10 to 15 per cent of the Serbian electorate. So as far as I was concerned, those were the elements that made him a prominent political figure in Serbia. Now, as to whether Mr. Seselj's words were eccentric or whether they jibed with what other political leaders, leaders of political parties in Serbia had to say, it's difficult to say. To my mind, they were not that different. The only difference was that Mr. Seselj's words were always much more direct whenever he espoused his political views. Leaders of other political parties or people who were in the Serbian authorities at the time expressed their views in a much more circumspect manner. Or to be more precise, they expressed them less openly. I'm talking about the political views in light of the political circumstances in the country at the time, and the country was facing break-up or in effect it was already undergoing the process of collapse. I don't know whether I've answered all your questions now. The question was quite long and I'm not quite sure whether I -- I've answered fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have, sir. You have been very clear, and I thank you for providing such precise answers. So what you are telling us is that Mr. Seselj was a no-nonsense political figure who was able to express in very direct and clear terms what many other politicians at the time said in a much more convoluted way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I said it was done in a more convoluted way, I meant Mr. Jovic or the late Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the leading politicians in Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so what was it that the political leaders in Serbia at the time were saying, some of them in a convoluted manner and Mr. Seselj in much more direct terms, what was the underlying message as far as you could perceive it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try and answer this question, although I'm not quite sure that what I'm about to say will be completely accurate. In the Serbian politics, politicians were always saying that they were trying to preserve Yugoslavia as it was, that this was the basic goal of the Serbian politics, and that the leaders of other republics which were at the time already independent internationally recognised states were doing the exact opposite, that they were trying to break Yugoslavia up. And that one of the instruments for the preservation of Yugoslavia was in fact the Yugoslav People's Army. Now, as to how the Yugoslav People's Army was actually used in the effort to preserve the collapsing state I think is more or less general knowledge. As far as I was able to follow the developments as they were presented on TV or in the press, of course this kind of conclusion could not be drawn. But the events that became quite clear later on showed that the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, was put to a completely different use, a use that was much more profitable for the Serbian political leaders at the time. It benefitted them much more, so I'm talking about the people in the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. My question to you, Mr. Witness, was rather more to try and understand how you perceived the underlying message that came out from the political Serbian leadership at the time. You told us that most of the politicians or the political leading figures were speaking in convoluted terms, but that Mr. Seselj was able to cut right through all those words and express in a clear and direct manner what this was all about. So my question to you was: Well, what was it about? What was the underlying message as far as you could perceive it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring in your question to Mr. Seselj only or to the leading politicians in the rump Yugoslavia? I don't think that I've understood your question. So are you talking about Mr. Seselj specifically or other people too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for being unclear. My answer to you is that if you're able to make a distinction between what other politicians said and what Mr. Seselj said in terms of the contents, then I would be interested to hear. But my question was actually generally put, namely, from the Serb political leadership what was the underlying message that came out in respect of the way in which the former Yugoslavia should be preserved? And as I said, if you can distinguish between what Mr. Seselj said and what other politicians said, that's fine; but if you can't, then I was interested in hearing just how you perceived the programme or the message that was disseminated in public at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to explain to you now how I saw things. In my opinion, and after all this was said what I'm about to share with you, what this was all about was about all Serbs living in a single state. This could be taken -- an effort to -- for that state to be Yugoslavia, but at the same time you could see it as an effort for all Serbs to live in a single state which would be, as it was termed then, Greater Serbia. And some former Yugoslav republics had already become independent states at the time, and in light of that fact, my opinion that it was in fact an effort to create a state which would be inhabited exclusively or in the majority by Serbs, that would be tantamount to Greater Serbia. And that means that parts of Croatia and parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be annexed to that state. I don't know if I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- did that also imply that non-Serbs would have to leave Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a certain number of people or even a large number of people - I was not aware of the figures at the time - of Serb ethnicity who lived in other republics, primarily Croatia, did leave Croatia at the relevant time, time relevant for my testimony. Of course I didn't know whether those people had been expelled or simply were refugees who had to flee in face of the fighting. But it is a fact that at the time the idea was already mooted that there should be an exchange of population. And I think that Mr. Seselj spoke to that effect in the Serbian Assembly, but as far as I can recall, he used other terms when he spoke about this issue. He talked about reciprocity, something that we could call reciprocity. So if a certain number of Serbs had to flee for any reason or was expelled from their homes, then Croats who during the war, the ethnic revolutions, lived in Serbia would have to suffer the same fate. That's how I understood things. If I'm not mistaken, this opinion was not created later, but I think that it was actually confirmed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, the way in which I understand you -- your testimony just now is that there was an interest on the Serbian side and perhaps also on the Croatian side to expel non-Serbs from the Serbian territory and to expel non-Croatians from the Republic of Croatia. And there was then a movement to accommodate on both sides people who were expelled from the other side. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is. The only difference is that other terms were used, human re-settlement of the population, humane re-settlement of the population. Well, it's really -- there's no need for us to make any comments as to how a re-settlement can be humane at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will get back to that in just a little minute, but if I can return to the question that I put to you just a while ago, namely, what was the underlying message that was sent out from the political leadership in Serbia? From what you have just told us, the understanding that I am able to make is that the message that was given from the Serbian political leadership was that non-Serbs should leave the territory which was perceived to belong to Serbs. And I just want to ask you if this is a correct understanding of your testimony or whether I have misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct. This perception applies only to the statements of some politicians, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was that also the perception expressed by Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember reading somewhere or maybe seeing on television if it was broadcast by Serbian TV a debate in the parliament, where Mr. Seselj stated that the same number of Serbs as had been expelled by Franjo Tudjman from Croatia must leave from the Republic of Serbia. The same number of people must leave Serbia. It's a primitive understanding of justice or maybe some sort of justice. When I mentioned the convoluted nature of some public appearances and speeches, I forgot to say in them the term "humane re-settlement" was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think the issue of whether or not the re-settlement was humane can be left to a later moment. At this point I have no further questions to you and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since I have not had my 40 minutes, I still have a little bit of time, a follow-up question for you. At some point you mentioned Mr. Sibincic. Can you tell us more specifically who this person was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In an effort to give you the most accurate and truthful answer about that man, I have to say I knew him only superficially. He spent his working hours outside of Hrtkovci and would only come back after his work was done. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to his ideas about national problems or political problems, I had no idea what he thought up until the time when Mr. Sibincic placed himself or was placed in the role of someone who would first be involved in the effort to admit Serbian refugees, which was commendable, but also later in the role of mediator and the person who pointed his finger at people with whom those refugees should negotiate about a possible swap of property. You could put it in other words, pointing his finger at people who should be pressured to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Sibincic, what political party did he belong to according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I found out, he was a member of the Serb Radical Party and their leader at the time was Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a last question but I would like to move into private session, otherwise we run the risk of identifying you. Registrar, can we move into private session -- into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before beginning, I'd like to discuss the article that you just discussed, specifically that article is, as the Court said, 14 May 1992, that's the date. That has been admitted into evidence as Exhibit P556, which is also in your binder as 65 ter 1309. And I should draw the Court's attention to the fact that this was an exhibit that was attached to the second statement that was given by this witness. It previously had a 65 ter number of 261, and that would appear on the last page of his 2006 statement to the Court -- to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My name is Lisa Biersay, and I appear on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. You and I, we have never met before, so I wanted to take the opportunity to introduce myself to you. What I would like to do is to first discuss something that was recently discussed with respect to Mr. Sibincic, and then I'd like to talk more about your personal background and history and then move closer to the events surrounding 1992, when you left Hrtkovci. You were asked about Mr. Sibincic's association with the SRS. How is it that you came to have that information about his affiliation with the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was the talk of the village. The village has 2.500, 3.000 inhabitants, a relatively small community. News spreads fast and not only news but all sorts of stories and rumours and information about anything that happens anywhere or to any inhabitant, especially if the event in question is so serious. So I did not ask Mr. Sibincic whether he was a member of the Serb Radical Party, but there were people who claimed that he was, even when I asked them directly. But I can't remember now who it was that I asked about it. I think -- I thought that the person who answered in the affirmative when I asked that question was well informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the name Rade Cakmak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how is it that you know that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was one of the people who had arrived from the territory of Croatia, fleeing from the war, I suppose, or maybe for some other reason. I really don't know anything for sure. I can only suppose. He started to be talked about in Hrtkovci as a man who was going to participate or was already involved in the expulsion of non-Serbs from Hrtkovci which had already begun. I never met the man and I have never even seen him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Based on what you know, what relationship, if any, was there between Rade Cakmak and Mr. Sibincic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again it's based on what I heard from other people. There existed some sort of co-operation between them. Some people said it was very close co-operation in affairs that I have just mentioned. In other words, a programme of expulsion of non-Serbs from Hrtkovci or getting them to move out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat, these are things that I only heard about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand, and it's very good that you -- you're precise about the source of your information and the Trial Chamber appreciates that. Could you tell us, if you know, whether or not Mr. Sibincic held an official political position in Hrtkovci in this time-period, April, May, June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until May 1992 I don't think he held any official position in the local authorities. In that period, that is to say, from mid-May until the final swap of property that I arranged with a Serb from Croatia, I was away a lot of the time travelling. And what exactly was going on in the local authorities on the local scene in Hrtkovci, I don't know, whether Sibincic had in the meantime acquired a role in the authorities, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But by the time you first started making your trips to Croatia to find a house for exchange purposes, by that time he was not a local authority or official in any capacity in Hrtkovci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's not correct or is what I said not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not, that's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name Nenad Canak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the name was familiar, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His views were quite contrary to the prevailing views at the time in what is normally called political opposition. From all I know, he was against what was going on in the former Yugoslavia at the time and in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "what was going on," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant the break-up of Yugoslavia using war as a means, military means.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to take you back in time away from those events, and we'll work back -- we'll work our way up to them again. You already described to the Trial Chamber that you were born -- when you were born. You were born in Hrtkovci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You were raised in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I finished primary school in Hrtkovci, that's the eight-year primary school; and I went to high school not far away, in a place called Ruma. And I did my university studies in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be careful, you run the risk of identifying the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long had your family, your family roots, how long had they been in Hrtkovci before you moved in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The accepted length of time was three centuries among us. My ancestors settled there during the settlements under the Carnojevici dynasty, when Albanians joined forces with the Austro-Hungarian empire against Turkey, and it was a time when Serbs and Albanians were withdrawing, those who had fought on the Austro-Hungarian side and feared Turkish Ottoman revenge, and they settled there sometime in the first half of the 17th century. I may be mistaken about the year, but I never thought of it as important enough to go and check. In any case, my ancestors lived there for a long time back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially if you look at it from the viewpoint of one lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The first wave of Serb refugees that you described who came to Hrtkovci, were they -- did they appear to be armed people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear or see anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, when the second wave came in April -- late April/early May of 1992, were those -- were some of those refugees armed, based on what you could see or on what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see some of those armed people myself. I heard about most of them, but I saw some of them. Those armed people started arriving either individually or in small groups even before that date that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And -- excuse me. When you say "before," how much earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some 10 or 15 days earlier. It's a long time -- it was a long time ago and I can't really recall all that specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to ask you an important follow-on question. Mrs. Biersay is asking you questions about the arrival of the refugees, and indeed, as she says, there was a first wave and then a second wave. As I'm listening to Mrs. Biersay I was also reading a document and I'd like you to give us your opinion on this document. You're not aware of this document, but it's important for Mrs. Biersay to know because she knows it. This is a report from the Ministry of Interior, Department of State Security, dated 4th of June, 1992, and I've got the number for the benefit of Mrs. Biersay, 1399. Now, the Ministry of Interior of the republic of --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, forgive me for interrupting. That's Exhibit Number P551 and it's also in your binder if you'd like to access it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. So this is Exhibit P551. All right. So, Witness, the Ministry of Interior is writing a report about the arrival of the refugees and explains at great length that they had arrived from Croatia, that some were armed, that there were paramilitary forces, and so on and so forth, and this was highlighted by Mrs. Biersay in her questions. Now, what I'm interested in is the following. A number of cases were mentioned and there's probably one case that you're not aware of in which refugees arriving from Croatia did not abide by the decisions of the authorities, and on the 1st of June, 1992, with the aid of the Serbian Radical Party they went on to create problems in a road which was under the responsibility of the Indjija municipality. Indjija, I don't know where this municipality is located. Now, this report states that measures must be taken. So Mr. Witness, you - and because you have seen the arrival of these refugees, you have seen what was the reaction of the authorities, and unless I'm mistaken, it is stated that there were only two policemen in your locality. However, in some reports those behaviours are criticised and the paramilitary forces, including the Serbian Radical Party's, are also criticised. Now, in your opinion, in June 1992 at the time, on the 1st of June, 1992, according to you, was the Serbian Radical Party in total agreement with the authorities of the time, including the president, unless I'm mistaken it was Slobodan Milosevic; or, as you see it, could it be that there were some disagreements? Can you answer this question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's really difficult for me to answer that question in any way that might be considered reliable. I really don't know whether Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic, as the president of Serbia, had opposing views of some issues or whether they worked together on some issues. The question that Madam Prosecutor asked me about the first wave of refugees where I tried to respond by saying for the most part these were peace-loving, unfortunate people who needed assistance. But based on what the Serbian Ministry of the Interior was writing about, violent, armed people, I don't know nothing about that. But later on this did indeed happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Okay. Well, while I have this document in front of me I'd like to ask you a question related to a previous question I asked you about Sibincic. Now the department of state security, which seems to be very well informed, states, white on black, that on the 15th of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation at all. Since you have started talking, I have not heard a single word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So we need to be assisted by technology here. Let me ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let me put the question again. Can you hear? Is it working now? Well, maybe it has to do with a problem of microphone. Right. So, Mr. Witness, as I said, I want to use this document while I have it -- is it still not working?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps the interpreter is silent. Maybe the interpreter could say a few words and then I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Can the interpreter say something so -- make sure as that Mr. Seselj receives the interpretation? Registrar, if there is a problem, maybe we can take a break now. Anyway, we were due to take a break at 12.30, so let's take a break a little earlier than planned and so technicians have the time to fix it. I have an important question to ask and I hope I don't forget about it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Witness, I'm going to put you a question based on this document which you do not know but this is not a problem. The state security department --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Since I don't have the commands for the headphones, I would like the volume for the interpretation to be turned up a little bit. I can no longer do that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I will be able to put my question. Let me start again for the sixth time. Witness, the state security department says in this document that Mr. Sibincic was at the time, on the 15th of May, 1992, one of the leaders of the SPO. You claimed that Mr. Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party. As far as you're concerned, are the SPO and the Serbian Radical Party the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my question, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying, no, no, it's not the same thing. How is it, then, that Mr. Sibincic according to these people well-versed in state security matters say that he is a member of the SPO, a leader of the SPO, and at the same time you say Mr. Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party? I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only explanation that I could provide is that I made a mistake. I couldn't say anything else really. So the information that I heard was obviously wrong and not in line with what you've just told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall see. I shall draw no conclusions thereof for the time being. I noticed that this document which stems from operatives who are specialists, they established this distinction between those -- between the SPO and the Serbian Radical Party. In the next paragraph, the Serbian Radical Party is mentioned, whereas in the previous paragraph the SPO is mentioned. That's it. Mrs. Biersay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect to this exhibit, which is Exhibit P551, just for the record it reads: "Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, state security department, Sremska Mitrovica, state security department centre." Could you describe to the Trial Chamber how far or how close Sremska Mitrovica is to Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's a question for you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15 to 16 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn your attention to the Assembly session that you discussed during the questions from the Trial Chamber, and in this regard, in connection to your 2006 statement you were shown three -- more than three, but specifically I want to address three of the items that you discussed in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: First if we could please have 65 ter 1062.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while that is being obtained, it is dated April 1st, 1992. The description is Vojislav Seselj's speech before Assembly of Serbia, published in Vojislav Seselj's book. The English is "Speeches of the Deputy, Belgrade 1993."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could have the second page in B/C/S so that the witness can see the actual beginning of the speech. And if we could now go to the third page in the B/C/S for the witness's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you generally recognise this speech as the one that you discussed -- one of the ones that you discussed in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well some -- I do recall some of the details from this speech, whether through the media, the press, or TV, I really don't know. But I do recall some of those things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if I could direct your attention specifically, I believe it is the B/C/S page 5. It would be the second paragraph under the heading "Vojislav Seselj." And I'll read the English which is on page 4, if we could go to page 4 of the English. And the first -- that line reads: "Mr. Skenderovic should know that, in international law there is a principle of retortion, which in the Serbian language means retaliation." Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then moving to the -- in the same section under "Vojislav Seselj," and we could move to the last sentence in the B/C/S -- I believe it would still be page 5. In English it's also page 5. And reading: "Croats in Slankamen, Zemun and other places will not be able to sleep a wink until they have moved out ..." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Madam Biersay, when she asks questions, cannot falsify the text itself and she's doing that by leaving out the beginning of this sentence here, which reads: "After the next or any other elections once the government" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is a point --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "changes Serbia" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- if he would like to read that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not completed my objection and I don't think it's admissible --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- he can. I am reading the English translation and he can wait for his turn in order to speak to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay cannot falsify the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're raising an objection. According to the Rules of this Tribunal, nothing relates to objections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have yet to present it, Mr. President. I began making my objection and Mrs. Biersay then simply butted in, as she usually does. She was supposed to read the beginning of the sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this might be a translation issue. You interrupted me when I hadn't even finished my sentence. I was saying that you raised an objection. I was saying that objections are not taken into account by our rules. This is an Anglo-Saxon practice where there is a sole Judge and a jury, and objections are made to avoid making an impression on a jury that is not a specialist in any field, and this is how the Judge can rule on the matter. In civil law countries the objection is, in fact, in the form of a remark made by a lawyer or an accused if the accused is self-representing himself when the person in question does not agree with what has just been said. And now you've said that Mrs. Biersay did not quote the text in its full context. Mrs. Biersay as a professional read the passage, but quite rightly she says that in the Anglo-Saxon system this is something which you could have raised during your cross-examination. Since we are all trying to be efficient to establish the truth we can make an effort and not stick to the examination-in-chief and cross-examination strictly. Since this is a different procedure, the witness is a witness of the Court, and therefore answers the Judges of this Court essentially. And you have been entitled, like the Prosecution has, to put questions. Your questions therefore cannot challenge the questions of the Judges. Mrs. Biersay, the problem runs as follows. You have quoted part of the intervention. Seemingly, this part should be read in its entirety. Could you make this effort from an intellectual standpoint to quote what the person has said in its entirety in this discussion with Mr. Seselj where he opposes what Mr. Seselj has said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: My question to the witness, because we are dealing in two different languages, is: Has he found in the B/C/S the part of the sentence that I've read. Once I have that affirmation, I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, did you find this part of the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, where is Slankamen and -- and Zemun --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm getting a French translation on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slankamen is a village in Vojvodina and Zemun is a town in Vojvodina, facing Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay, Slankamen is a village in Vojvodina and Zemun is a town in Vojvodina, not far removed from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So if I could now read the sentence to you in full. "Croats in Slankamen, Zemun, and other places will not be able to sleep a wink until they have moved out, because we have to accommodate Serbian refugees from Zagreb, Rijeka," forgive me for my pronunciation, "Varazdin and other Croatian towns, and put roofs over their heads and compensate them for the damages they have suffered in being expelled from their homes." When you described, Mr. Witness, to the Trial Chamber that you had information --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do I now have the right to make an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is it you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say that Mrs. Biersay is again falsifying facts. She must not do that. It says clearly here after these or some future elections, when we come into power, and that's the point of this whole passage, when we come into power, we'll do this and that. That's also the point of what I said in Hrtkovci. When we come into power, we will give each Serbian refugee the address of a Croat and we'll let -- we'll have them swap properties. I am explaining my programme, my platform, and what we will do when we come into power. And this is an obvious example that Mrs. Biersay is falsifying what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay, I don't have the exact text before me, but it seems that what you are describing is a situation which would be correct if Mr. Seselj were to come to power. This is not a reality. This is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand very well that's what he says. He's testifying instead of raising a legitimate procedural point, and I -- as the Court can see, I'm reading from the English translation. If he has an issue, then he can raise that with the Court or with the witness during his time. The Court can clearly see the sentence that I'm reading from page 5 of the English version at the top of the page. So may I continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing. I think deliberately the English page does not fit the Serbian page because what I am pointed out as being falsified by Mrs. Biersay is on the next page of the English. And these are cheap tricks by the Prosecutor, cheap tricks that have no place in a serious judicial system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Biersay, I don't know what the situation is. I assume you are of good faith. What matters is to know what actually happened. Perhaps the witness can answer this. Put your question. I and my colleagues remember what Mr. Seselj has just said, and when he puts his questions I believe he will address us again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have a proposal, if Mr. Seselj seems to think that somehow I've -- and the Office of the Prosecutor has doctored this exhibit, I'd propose that the witness read that last sentence in his language, if he's able to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is precisely the point. Why just the last sentence? Why not the one before too? Let the witness read from the sentence that begins with: "After these or some future elections ..." This is the second sentence in this paragraph, and then the sense would not be falsified.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He can have the witness do that during his time. During my time, during the Prosecution's time, I would propose that the witness read it -- the one sentence in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed and put your question, Mrs. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you look at this and in the context of what you previously told the Trial Chamber about hearing what Mr. Seselj said about expelling Croats in return for the expulsion of Serbs from Croatia, is this what you meant, this document? Is this what you had in mind, the information in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is. That is a question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant and that is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of 65 ter 1062, which is the excerpt from Mr. Seselj's book. We would also tender the complete minutes of the speech, not just of his speech but of the session, and that is 65 ter 1065, and that's where 1062 comes from. So we would tender both of those exhibits at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber always rules on the admission of documents after the cross-examination. We have noted your request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I agree completely. This is obviously exculpatory material for me, so there's no controversy. It can be admitted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. We shall ask the Registrar, since Mr. Seselj so wishes, to give us an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 01062 shall be assigned Exhibit P892. 65 ter document 01065 shall be assigned Exhibit P893. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you also discussed with the Trial Chamber seeing and hearing about media coverage of Mr. Seselj, and specifically with respect to the April 1st, 1992, Assembly session. I'd like to play you a clip that was also showed to you -- shown to you in conjunction with your November 2006 statement. And that is currently MFI P16, which is also 65 ter 6011 for easy reference in your -- in the Court's binders. I hope you'll be able to see the clip from where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This can't be shown for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I can move on to another topic and we can -- and I hear that it's now ready. So if we could please try to play this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't have the translation in French. We've seen the English subtitles, but the problem is that we see Mr. Seselj taking the floor but the commentary comes from a journalist. Is her running commentary exactly the same as what Mr. Seselj was saying? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may be of assistance. We heard this dispute once before when there was another witness related to Hrtkovci and this videotape. It's all about interpretation. You have it all in the two documents you admitted, an excerpt from my book and a broader excerpt from the parliament transcript. This is an interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this discussion -- testifying by Mr. Seselj. The -- he's absolutely right --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- he's absolutely right that it was previously presented to the Court. The issue was context. This witness has described for the Court hearing about press coverage, and so this is just about that. And I certainly understand that it will be for the Court and the Court only to decide whether or not what is being said about the speech is accurate or not, but the purpose with respect to this witness is to get him to say whether or not this was an example of the press coverage that he described for the Trial Chamber. That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is an example of the sort of forgery the Prosecution resorts to. This is the programme from the Croatian television that the witness was not able to see in Hrtkovci. The witness could have seen the direct Serbian broadcast from the parliament session and he could hear all that I said and all the other MPs said in the parliament. And the programme from Croatian TV was not something he could have watched in April 1992. However, the Croat journalist is fairer than Mrs. Biersay. He says correctly that I said "after the next elections when we come into power." The Croatian journalist is fairer than Mrs. Biersay, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, Mr. Seselj, according to what Mrs. Biersay is saying, what she's trying to highlight is the media coverage of things which you may have said. And she's using this video that also includes the comment of a journalist and she's probably going to ask the witness whether he heard the comment made by the journalist or whether he heard your speech before the Assembly. And of course, yeah, there may be a difference here but we'll only find out through the witness's answer. So keep going, Mrs. Biersay, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, and this time this is a question for you, could you tell us whether this is the type of media coverage of the Assembly session that you described hearing about from other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean what the journalist said, the journalist of the Belgrade TV, that's correct; but precisely this passage that is concerned here, I heard that in its entirety on Belgrade television.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we'd move for the admission of what is now MFI P16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There is no grounds for admission. Still today the Prosecution can ask from the Serbian government a recording of my entire speech in the parliament in 1992 because it is all carefully archived, both the transcript and the video recording. The transcript is already in evidence, you just admitted it. A journalist's interpretation cannot replace the original, and the witness just said he heard the speech in its entirety. This is really inadmissible conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Chamber decides that a decision shall be made at a later stage. I just wish to say that the comment from the journalist refers to the elections, what's going to happen after the election. That is written black on white, and this corresponds to what Mr. Seselj was saying. Mrs. Biersay, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn your attention to the second wave of armed Serb refugees that you talked about previously. I believe that you described when they started coming to Hrtkovci. Could you remind the Chamber of the date that -- as far as you remember it, of that happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've already said this before. They started coming in individually and in smaller groups. Armed men of intimidating demeanour started arriving in Hrtkovci even before this speech by Mr. Seselj, and after the speech they were coming in in larger numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we please go into private session for this question that I have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right then. The hearing is now over. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
